1.pericope_label: The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him: it is not for kings to drink wine: open thy mouth for the dumb

schools.summary: Henry takes Lemuel for Solomon on the sense of the name and on the parallel with what his father taught him, draws from the passage that mothers as well as fathers must teach their children while they are most under the mother’s eye, adds that even kings must be catechised since the greatest of men is less than the least of the ordinances of God, and makes the second verse a chiding question from a mother who had observed her son’s inclination to women and wine.

Gill reports three answers to the question who Lemuel was, a later king, a foreign prince taught by a Jewish mother, and Solomon, whom the general sense of Jewish and Christian writers prefers; he hears the broken exclamation as a mother confessing she wants words and wants wisdom; and he turns the strong drink of the sixth verse into almsgiving, kings giving it away out of their abundance to those in starving circumstances rather than drinking it themselves.

Clarke refuses the identification with Solomon on two grounds, that the son is called the son of my womb, which suits a first-born rather than the child of a woman who had been another man’s wife, and the son of my vows, which intimates a lawful marriage; he takes the opening particle as a preposition, so that the words are spoken to the king rather than by him, calls the second verse very elliptical and quotes an old English version that fills it out, and lists the renderings proposed for those appointed to destruction; Wesley assents to Solomon by general consent and reads the exclamation as a heart too full to begin.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the pointing of the third verse allows an infinitive that would make it a warning against wars of invasion, and refuse it because such a warning will not parallel one against spending strength on women; they report, with Ellicott, that on the ground of the sixth verse the women of the city prepared a drugged draught for those condemned to death, which was offered to Jesus and refused because he would not pass from life insensible to his suffering; Ellicott reads the superscription as Lemuel, king of Massa, denies that the name designates Solomon, and sets the passage among Eastern manners where the mother of a king holds the rank of queen-mother.

debates: Who was Lemuel? Gill canvasses a later king and a foreign prince before settling with the general sense of Jewish and Christian writers on Solomon, and Henry and Wesley agree. Ellicott reads the line as Lemuel, king of Massa, and says the identification with Solomon has no good reason. Clarke refuses it outright, arguing that the son of my womb suits a first-born rather than the child of a woman who had been another man’s wife, and that the son of my vows intimates a lawful marriage; he also takes the opening particle as a preposition, making these words spoken to the king rather than by him.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott independently report the same custom from the sixth verse, that the women of the city prepared a drugged draught for the condemned, which was offered to Jesus and refused because he would not pass from life insensible to his suffering.
Ellicott brings the veneration of the queen-mother down to his own day, noting that the mother of the ruler of Egypt ranks before his principal wife.
Henry observes that even kings must be catechised, since the greatest of men is less than the least of the ordinances of God.
Keil and Delitzsch consider and reject a pointing that would turn the third verse into a warning against wars of invasion, on the ground that it will not parallel the warning about women.
themes: a king three commentators cannot place
words to the king or from him
a mother who cannot begin
a cup prepared for the condemned
a widow named from dumbness

10.pericope_label: Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies: the heart of her husband doth safely trust in her: she seeketh wool, and flax

schools.summary: Henry counts the twenty-two verses and reports that the alphabetical form makes some take the poem for a separate piece, commonly repeated among the pious Jews and made alphabetical for ease of remembering, finds its abridgment in two apostolic passages on the duty of wives, and quotes the household proverb that he who will thrive must ask his wife leave.

Gill reports that two versions detach this passage and that a scholar makes it another hand’s composition, suggests that the mother supplied the substance and the son the artificial form, holds that the description can agree with no daughter of fallen Adam taken literally, and collects the great personages of antiquity who spun with their own hands, with the custom of leading newly married women home behind a distaff and spindle.

Clarke sets out the acrostic and divides the piece into the general character, its particulars and the summing up, glosses the opening word as a woman of power and strength full of mental energy, draws from the spoil of the eleventh verse the picture of a husband under no necessity of predatory excursions at the expense of neighbouring tribes, and keeps the trade of the fourteenth verse exact, that if she imports she exports; Wesley notes the alphabetical order and makes the husband free of indirect courses to get wealth.

Keil and Delitzsch explain the word for spoil as what is taken from an enemy but come to mean gain of any kind, and reject a scholar who makes it the husband’s prosperity rather than the gain his wife brings in; they praise the constancy of the twelfth verse as a love not dependent on freaks but resting on deep moral grounds, dispute the verb of the thirteenth against five scholars who make it merely handling wool and flax, and admire in the fourteenth a calculating look that goes beyond the nearest circle; Ellicott lists the mystical identifications held at different times, the Law, the Church and the Holy Spirit, and reads the fourteenth verse as buying cheaply at a distance.

debates: Whose poem is this, and about whom? Gill reports that two versions detach it and that a scholar assigns it to another hand, and proposes that the mother gave the substance and the son the alphabetical form; Henry reports the same suspicion, that the acrostic marks a separate piece already current among the pious. On the subject, Gill denies that any daughter of fallen Adam can answer the description literally and rejects the application to the Virgin; Ellicott lists the Law, the Church and the Holy Spirit as identifications held at different times without adopting one; Clarke and Wesley keep to a woman.
outliers: Henry quotes a household proverb of his own day, that he who will thrive must ask his wife leave.
Clarke reads the promise about spoil as freeing the husband from predatory excursions at the expense of the neighbouring tribes, where the others read only profit.
Gill supports the spinning of the thirteenth verse from Roman antiquity, including a matron found spinning with her maids when her husband came from the camp, and the distaff carried before a bride.
Keil and Delitzsch insist that the verb of the thirteenth verse describes the mind’s intention and not the hand’s work, against five scholars who render it that she handles wool and flax.
themes: a poem built on the alphabet
a woman no daughter of Adam can match
spoil that becomes gain
a queen at the distaff
a household that trades abroad

15.pericope_label: She riseth also while it is yet night, and giveth meat to her household: she considereth a field, and buyeth it: she layeth her hands to the spindle

schools.summary: Gill compares the rising while it was yet dark to Christ rising to pray, makes the field of the sixteenth verse the Scriptures, which the enlightened will buy at any rate and never sell, reads the merchandise of the eighteenth as trading to heaven, and notes that a queen of the Greek poems and her maidens plied the spindle as she does.

Clarke makes her an economist of time whose household rises before daylight, distinguishes the food given to those going out from the task given to the women within, supposes a growing family needing more land and a neighbouring field bought a good bargain, reads the girding as care of her own health, and offers three explanations of the lamp that burns all night, ending with a protest that little children are so employed now to fill the coffers of their unfeeling taskmasters; Wesley will not press the candle beyond her unwearied care, and observes that unmarried women are still called spinsters in the language of our law.

Keil and Delitzsch place her rising before the other inmates but not before the maids, since care for her house stands above her own comfort, suggest that the field was one hitherto wanting to a family whose husband is no landlord but has a business in the city, follow the surplus produce to market and make the gain the spur of her diligence, and describe the whorl fixed on the spindle to give it weight and regulate its movement; Ellicott notes that what is given to the maidens may be either their provisions or their work, and reads the field as bought with her savings.

debates: What is the portion given to the maidens? Ellicott allows both senses, the allotted provisions or the allotted work, without choosing. Clarke divides the verse between the two, food for those going out to the fields and the flocks and a task for the women employed within, which fixes the kind of work, the material and the quantity expected of each. Keil and Delitzsch take the fixed portion as food and use the verse to establish the order of the household, since she is up before the rest but not before the maids.
outliers: Clarke turns from the lamp burning all night to his own century, protesting that little children are now employed at such night work to support indigent parents and fill the coffers of their unfeeling taskmasters.
Wesley derives a term of English law from the nineteenth verse, that unmarried women are called spinsters because such employments were not once beneath great persons.
Keil and Delitzsch infer the husband’s occupation from the purchase of the field, since the poet has in view a woman whose husband is no landlord but has a business in the city.
Clarke observes that barter rather than buying is her chief mode of traffic, whatever goes out bringing its worth in.
themes: a household awake before daylight
food for the field and a task for the house
a field bought out of savings
a lamp that shames its own century
the law’s word for an unmarried woman

20.pericope_label: She stretcheth out her hand to the poor: she is not afraid of the snow for her household: her husband is known in the gates: she maketh fine linen, and selleth it

schools.summary: Gill reports a version that renders the coverings garments of divers colours like the coat of the patriarch’s son, gives two Jewish opinions on why the husband is known in the gates, one for the garments she made him and one for his own wisdom, and reports a commentator who makes the linen of the last verse a covering for the night, with a version that adds the city she sells to.

Clarke distinguishes the one hand held out to the poor in general from the two hands given to the afflicted poor and holds that God requires a portion for the poor out of every man’s gain, refuses the rendering scarlet since a colour cannot keep off cold and the word means double garments, identifies her linen with the fine cloth he has seen wrapping mummies, and doubts the story that purple was dyed from a shellfish, taking it for an invention to hide the trade secret; Wesley notes that she has provided not merely for necessity but for delight and ornament.

Keil and Delitzsch deny that alms are meant in the twentieth verse, since the hand is held out as if for an alliance and the word denotes only the half-opened hand, note that snow in that country is sometimes accompanied by intense cold, give four old renderings of the coverings, hold that such a wife advances the estimation in which her husband is held, and trace the word for linen in the last verse to a distant country and to a light garment worn on the bare body; Ellicott allows either sympathy or alms at the twentieth verse, keeps scarlet as a colour suggesting warmth, and observes that the husband, having no domestic anxieties, is free for public life.

debates: What are the household clothed in? Ellicott keeps the received scarlet and makes the colour itself suggest warmth and comfort; Keil and Delitzsch keep it too and derive the word from a root meaning to shine. Clarke refuses it, arguing that a colour can do nothing against cold and would be improper wear for the bogs and dirt of winter, and that the word, from a root meaning to double, denotes double garments — a rendering he notes the translators themselves placed in the margin.
outliers: Clarke doubts the ancient account of purple dye, having seen the shellfish it is said to come from and holding the story an invention to conceal the trade secret of dyeing.
Keil and Delitzsch read the outstretched hand as an offer of alliance rather than of alms, the gesture saying, place confidence in me, there thou hast my hand.
Clarke identifies the fine linen with the cloth he has often seen wrapping the bodies of mummies, and compares it to our coarse calico.
Gill preserves a version that names the city to which she sells her linen, where the others leave the buyers unnamed.
themes: one hand for the poor, two for the afflicted
scarlet or a second suit of clothes
a dye whose story is doubted
a husband at leisure for public life
linen named from a distant country

25.pericope_label: Strength and honour are her clothing: she openeth her mouth with wisdom: she looketh well to the ways of her household: her children arise up, and call her blessed

schools.summary: Gill takes the clothing of strength for the church, weak in herself and strong in her Lord, reads the oversight of the household ecclesiastically so that all things are done decently and in order, the feeble supported and the incorrigible cast out, and reports a Jewish note that the children rise in the morning because her lamp had not gone out in the night, with another that takes them for disciples.

Clarke reads the strength and honour of her clothing as the double perfection of her workmanship, strong and elegant, so that she will never blush for anything she has made or worn or sold, denies that she is a drudge since she has not neglected the cultivation of her mind, makes a religious industry the law of her house where all are fed well that they may work well, and puts a good education next to divine influence in accounting for children who rise up and pay respect; Wesley takes the strength for magnanimity and courage and the laughter for tranquillity resting on providence, and marks the two extremes of speech she avoids.

Keil and Delitzsch define strength as power over the changes of temporal circumstance and glory as elevation above the low and common, call the twenty-sixth verse one of the most beautiful features in the portrait and distinguish what lies under the tongue from what is on it, take its phrase as a genitive of property against a scholar who reads it as instruction towards kindliness, derive the word for ways from a root meaning the walk, and announce the finale at the twenty-eighth verse, where the rising up carries the idea of reverential honour; Ellicott makes the clothing serve for protection and ornament, renders the second clause that she smiles at the coming day, and denies that she is a mere household drudge.

debates: What is the law of kindness on her tongue? Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase as a genitive of property, so that the instruction itself is amiable, and reject a scholar who reads it as instruction directed towards kindliness. Ellicott makes kindness the law by which she regulates all her words. Wesley explains why the word law is used at all, since the practice is constant and customary and proceeds from an inward principle; Clarke reads the verse chiefly as evidence that her mind has been cultivated.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch single out the twenty-sixth verse as one of the most beautiful features in the whole portrait, the only such judgment any of them passes on a verse of this poem.
Clarke explains the feeding of the household from the working of it, that they are fed well in order that they may work well, and that idleness leads to vice.
Ellicott and Clarke both use the twenty-sixth verse to deny that the woman is a household drudge with no thought beyond food and clothing.
Gill reports a Jewish note connecting the children rising with the lamp of the eighteenth verse, since they rise in the morning and her light had not gone out in the night.
themes: strength as power over circumstance
a smile at the coming day
wisdom breaking the silence of a mouth
fed well that they may work well
a finale in which the house rises

29.pericope_label: Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all: favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: give her of the fruit of her hands

schools.summary: Gill reports the versions that render the twenty-ninth verse of gathering riches without rejecting them, turns the many daughters into false churches where the true church is one, applies the deceitful favour to the dressings of the church he opposes, and reports two Jewish readings of the last verse, one making it the husband’s charge to the children and the other referring it to the world to come.

Clarke assigns the twenty-ninth verse to the husband and renders its second line that she has ascended above the whole of them, then steps out of the commentary to say he has met at least her equal in the daughter of one divine and the wife of another; he holds that grace of manner may be an outward varnish learned by drilling in polished seminaries and lasting only while the restraint lasts, suggests that the last verse may be a prayer rather than a charge, and ends his comment with an Amen; Wesley makes comeliness often a cover to a deformed soul, soon lost by diseases and contingencies as well as by death.

Keil and Delitzsch refuse the rendering that makes the many daughters gainers of riches, which six authorities adopt, since it would give the encomium a mercenary note and the phrase bears that sense only with a preposition of the person; they hold that the thirtieth verse is not the husband’s continued praise, as three scholars take it, but the poet’s own closing sentence, grace being deceit because a man who judges by appearance is deceived and beauty vanity because it falls under the law of all material things; and they explain the fruit of her hands as the good her conduct has brought to maturity. Ellicott glosses the daughters as women, a term of affection, and grounds enduring praise in the fear of the Lord.

debates: Who speaks the thirtieth verse? Keil and Delitzsch deny that it continues the husband’s praise, as three scholars take it, and make it the poet’s own closing sentence, added to refer the husband’s words to their general ground. Clarke keeps the twenty-ninth verse for the husband and treats what follows as the summing up of the whole character. Gill leaves the speaker unsettled and reads the words of the church he opposes; Ellicott states the moral without asking whose it is.
outliers: Clarke leaves the text at the twenty-ninth verse to say that he has met at least this woman’s equal, the daughter of one divine and the wife of another, the rector of a country parish.
Keil and Delitzsch reject a rendering held by six named authorities on the ground that it would give the poem, at the height of its praise, a mercenary note.
Clarke traces deceitful grace of manner to the schoolroom, calling it a thing learned by painful drilling in polished seminaries and lasting only while the restraint lasts.
Clarke closes his comment on the book with an Amen, having asked that this example be set before every wife and mother.
themes: bravery, not the gaining of riches
a commentator naming a woman he knew
manners drilled and manners grown
beauty under the law of material things
a charge that may be a prayer
